sentences.text: The Mascarene parrot measured 35 cm in length with a wingspan of 211 mm, a tail ranging from 144 to 152 mm, a culmen of 32 to 36 mm, and a tarsus of 22 to 24 mm.
It featured red legs and naked red skin around its eyes and nostrils, while stuffed specimens show a brown body and a bluish head.
In 1674, the traveler Dubois described live birds as "petit-gris," a color resembling the dark phase of the red squirrel.
The species was first mentioned by French traveler Sieur Dubois in his 1674 travelogue of Réunion.
It was scientifically described as Psittacus mascarinus by Carl Linnaeus in 1771.
Today, only two stuffed specimens exist, located in collections in Paris and Vienna.
X-ray comparisons reveal that subfossil bones were intermediate in measurements between modern specimens and the stuffed ones.
Because several individuals were kept in captivity, the bird was likely not a specialized feeder, and a 1705 description by Jean Feuilley suggests it fattened itself seasonally.

The genus name Mascarinus prevailed, and when combined with the specific name mascarinus in 1891, it formed a tautonym; the IOC World Bird List emended the binomial name to M. mascarin in 2016, but the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature conserved M. mascarinus as a justified emendation in 2020.
The Mascarene parrot was endemic to the island of Réunion in the western Indian Ocean.
The last known account of wild birds on Réunion dates to the 1770s.
It is recorded as extinct in 1834 and was the last endemic bird species to go extinct on the island, preceding the hoopoe starling which disappeared in the mid-19th century.

The date and cause of extinction are unclear; while 1834 is the latest record, it is considered dubious, suggesting extinction likely occurred before 1800 or even earlier. Early writers incorrectly claimed the parrot was found on Madagascar, leading Lesson to propose the synonym Mascarinus madagascariensis in 1831. Some authors associated an unidentified dark parrot seen in Africa by Hasselqvist with the Mascarene parrot, but descriptions differ, leading to invalid name combinations, and it is debated whether this unidentified dark parrot was actually a grey parrot.
